name: Authoritarian conservatism
summary: Authoritarian conservatism defends order, hierarchy, tradition and religion, and accepts strong, often unelected central authority and forcible suppression of revolutionaries to keep them. It is nationalist and anti-communist but traditionalist rather than revolutionary, which separates it from fascism. Its economics vary from corporatism to laissez-faire.
scope: The conservative authoritarian right, as Payne defines it: the interwar and later European (and Latin and East Asian) right-wing regimes and movements that are authoritarian but not fascist. They rest on traditional religion rather than vitalism or secular neo-idealism, avoid radical breaks in legal and social continuity, favour a reorganised monarchism or neo-Catholic corporatism, keep elites and strong leadership tied to traditional legitimacy, and aim to freeze much of the existing social structure while weakening the organized proletariat (Payne, s1; Spielvogel, s3; Nelis et al., s7). Its intellectual root is the counter-revolutionary, ultra-royalist, ultramontane line of Joseph de Maistre (s2, s3) and Donoso Cortés (s4), as distinct from Burke's Whig conservatism. Regimes the defining sources tie to it: Salazar's Estado Novo (s1, s5), Franco's Spain (s6, s7), Horthy's Hungary, Pilsudski's Poland, Vichy and the Hindenburg-Papen conservative right (Payne's table 1.2, s1). Excludes fascism and the radical right (which Payne separates from it), the wider mainstream conservative tradition (Burke, Oakeshott, SEP's account of conservatism), and libertarian conservatism. Economics are not part of the core: Payne notes only that these groups almost without exception professed corporatism.
